The timer fires 1 minute after it starts, 2 minutes after boot, then 10 minutes after each tick finishes, and output goes to the journal. Each repo gets one driver. Installing the timer enables it and checks that systemd reports it enabled, then removes this repo's crontab lines, including entries written before the marker comment existed, and prints each removed line. `install-cron` reads its entry back and then disables this repo's timer. Commented-out lines, other repos' lines and unit files aida did not write are never touched, and a unit file of the same name that aida did not write is never overwritten. `aida schedule uninstall-systemd` disables only the timer (a running tick finishes) and deletes the two unit files. Both install commands need a person at an interactive terminal who answers yes. `aida doctor` counts either driver, and flags a repo where both are installed. <!-- trace:TASK-1491 | ai:claude -->

trace_lines.text: **Mail latency.** Each tick measures, per known recipient, how long the oldest unread message has waited. A known recipient is a seat or role in the agent registry, a team roster member or an active work session's owner or role; mail to any other address is ignored and never pages. Past `mail_latency` (`30m`) it notifies the operator through `aida notify` (never the mailbox or a chat), once per episode per recipient, again only after that recipient's mail is read and falls behind again. One notification names at most five recipients, then "+N more". <!-- trace:TASK-1492 | ai:claude -->

trace_lines.text: On Linux, `aida schedule install-systemd` installs a systemd user timer instead: `~/.config/systemd/user/aida-tick-<hash>.{service,timer}`, running the same `aida schedule tick` command from the repo with the same `PATH`. The timer fires 1 minute after it starts, 2 minutes after boot, then 10 minutes after each tick finishes, and output goes to the journal. Each repo gets one driver. Installing the timer enables it and checks that systemd reports it enabled, then removes this repo's crontab lines, including entries written before the marker comment existed, and prints each removed line. `install-cron` reads its entry back and then disables this repo's timer. Commented-out lines, other repos' lines and unit files aida did not write are never touched, and a unit file of the same name that aida did not write is never overwritten. `aida schedule uninstall-systemd` disables only the timer (a running tick finishes) and deletes the two unit files. Both install commands need a person at an interactive terminal who answers yes. `aida doctor` counts either driver, and flags a repo where both are installed. <!-- trace:TASK-1491 | ai:claude -->

Verbs: `aida shift tick [--dry-run] [--json]` (`--dry-run` prints the exact wave command, the specs, every guard with its value and where the switch was read, and writes nothing — the preflight), `aida shift status [--json]`, `aida shift enable`, `aida shift disable`, `aida shift resume`, `aida shift install --systemd-user|--cron` (enable, and install that driver in the same step; the repo's other driver is removed once the new one is verified). <!-- trace:TASK-1491 | ai:claude -->

trace_lines.text: **Mail latency.** Each tick measures, per known recipient, how long the oldest unread message has waited. A known recipient is a seat or role in the agent registry, a team roster member or an active work session's owner or role; mail to any other address is ignored and never pages. Past `mail_latency` (`30m`) it notifies the operator through `aida notify` (never the mailbox or a chat), once per episode per recipient, again only after that recipient's mail is read and falls behind again. One notification names at most five recipients, then "+N more". <!-- trace:TASK-1492 | ai:claude -->
